scope: 18 development cases; manual comparison against supplied evidence, not held-out accuracy
scale: Overall candidate versus baseline: better, worse, or no_clear_change. Better does not mean fully correct.

cases.notes: Both recaps list ten headlines in one long paragraph and connect a named player to an ambiguous record-signing teaser. Theme guidance does not resolve the ambiguity.
Candidate covers more headlines initially, then repeats its season summary across several paragraphs and adds broad performance judgments. Baseline is narrow but avoids the repetition loop.
Outputs are identical: both merge the matching praise reports but omit a separate player story and omit publisher attribution in prose.
Outputs are identical. Both expand abbreviated team names beyond source wording and strengthen an indicated jersey-number change in the hook.

Candidate abstains on a jersey-history headline; baseline invents a current legacy/recall framing for retrospective material. This is a defensible abstention, not proof that retrospective coverage must always be discarded.
Both abstain on the prediction/result packet.
Both falsely describe the head coach as fired, reversing the actor relationship in reporting about staff changes. Candidate slightly improves the qualification of an unrelated speculative trade.

Candidate passes strict validation but contradicts itself about whether an agent is named, invents a prerequisite for negotiations, and omits a distinct potential-team-interest story. Acceptance masks a factual regression.
Both interpret a Champions League reunion as a possible employment move and produce an unsupported structured finding.
Outputs are identical. Prose keeps the stories separate, but findings attach an unnamed-target quote to a named counterparty and the wrong report index.
Both turn a possible departure after a stated year into an unsupported contract-expiry claim.
Both overstate hypothetical trade coverage and lead with stored roster metadata. Baseline misattributes a trade idea; candidate invents an outlet's nationality and omits that idea.

Candidate turns an emergency-quarterback headline into quarterback errors, infers confidence from betting-favorite status, and ends the hook with a stray character. Both retain the same overall score.
Candidate invents a speaker's club affiliation, transfers outlet wording to another speaker, and invents fan anticipation in its hook. Baseline also adds unsupported tactical/cultural interpretation.
Both give anger and disappointment a mixed score of 50 and include a touchdown highlight that supplies no emotional reaction. Search/tone guidance does not correct the score meaning.
Candidate clarifies whose game plan was disrupted and keeps the distinct MVP-frustration thread while covering the scoring headline. Grouped attribution remains imperfect.
Candidate stays closer to the reported promise to improve and uses a more concrete hook, avoiding some added interpretation. Improvement is modest.
Both resolve an ambiguous win headline into a victory for the named opposing club without enough evidence.

deployment_assessment: No general quality improvement established. Keep the combined prompt experimental; production remains paused.
